questions.q: An alarm is configured with evaluation periods of 3 and datapoints to alarm of 2. What does that actually mean?
options: It fires only if at least 2 of the last 3 evaluation periods breached the threshold, tolerating one noisy period
It fires only after the metric has breached the threshold for 2 consecutive hours
It fires the instant any single data point ever breaches the threshold, regardless of the other two settings
It averages the last 3 periods into one value and never looks at individual periods again
questions.explain: This is an M-of-N alarm: it looks back over N (3) evaluation periods and fires only if M (2) of them breached the threshold — a deliberate middle ground between over-reacting to one blip and missing a real trend.

questions.q: With TreatMissingData left on its default setting, what happens if a per-instance metric stops reporting because the instance was terminated during a scale-in event?
options: The alarm is automatically deleted along with the instance
CloudWatch automatically treats the gap as notBreaching and the alarm clears immediately
The metric is recreated from the last known Auto Scaling group average
The default 'missing' treatment can leave a stale ALARM state in place even though nothing is actually wrong, which is a classic false-page source
questions.explain: The default missing treatment is easy to get wrong for a metric tied to an ephemeral resource; an alarm left on default during a scale-in can fire or stay in ALARM purely because the instance and its metric no longer exist.

questions.q: Why does a single threshold alarm tend to flap on a metric like p99 latency that legitimately hovers near its threshold?
options: CloudWatch alarms are hard-capped at firing once per hour, which causes a backlog of delayed notifications
Flapping only happens when the wrong AWS region is selected for the alarm
A metric bouncing just above and just below the threshold flips the alarm between OK and ALARM repeatedly, each transition potentially firing a notification
Composite alarms are required before any single-metric alarm is allowed to evaluate
questions.explain: A borderline metric (e.g. bouncing between 480ms and 520ms against a 500ms threshold) causes repeated OK/ALARM transitions, and each transition can notify — turning a not-actually-broken metric into a frequently paging alarm.

questions.q: What does a CloudWatch composite alarm actually monitor?
options: A single metric evaluated with two different statistics at once
The states of other CloudWatch alarms, combined with an AlarmRule expression using AND, OR, and NOT
The AWS billing dashboard's current monthly spend
The health of the CloudWatch service itself, independent of any customer-defined alarm
questions.explain: A composite alarm doesn't watch a metric directly — its AlarmRule expression combines the ALARM/OK states of other alarms, so it only enters ALARM when the logical condition over those underlying alarms is met.

questions.q: Given the AlarmRule `ALARM("elevated-5xx-rate") AND NOT ALARM("deployment-in-progress")`, when does this composite alarm actually notify on-call?
options: Whenever a deployment starts, regardless of the 5xx error rate
Only when the 5xx error rate is elevated AND no deployment is currently marked in progress, so a deploy's expected brief error blip doesn't page anyone
Every time the elevated-5xx-rate alarm changes state, even if a deployment is in progress
Never — NOT expressions inside an AlarmRule disable the composite alarm entirely
questions.explain: The NOT ALARM("deployment-in-progress") clause gates the real alert: elevated error rates during a known, flagged deployment window don't trigger the composite, but the same error rate outside a deployment window does.
